faqs.q: What should I include on a handyman estimate?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name and license number, the client and job-site address, a dated line-item list (call-out fee, labor, repairs, materials), a validity date, deposit terms, and a note that it is not a final invoice.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate the deposit automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantities and rates, and the subtotal, 25% deposit and balance due update automatically.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

deepDive.heading: Handyman estimating in practice: pricing models, license limits and deposits
deepDive.sub: How working handymen actually structure quotes — the difference between a quote that gets signed and one that starts a dispute.

blocks.h3: The three pricing models handymen put on estimates
paras: Handyman work is priced three ways, and the estimate should make it obvious which one applies — because the customer's trust depends on knowing how the number can move.
list: Time and materials (T&M): call-out fee plus labor hours plus materials at cost-plus. Most flexible, most common for diagnosis-style jobs where you cannot know the scope until you open it up. The estimate lists your hourly rate and states that hours will be confirmed before final billing.

Flat rate by task: a fixed price per job — 'replace garbage disposal: $220 installed'. Easiest to sell, easiest to compare, and the one Yelp-era customers have come to expect. The estimate must scope tightly: what is included, what triggers a re-quote.
Day rate: a single number for a full day of a punch-list. Fits the honey-do list jobs — a morning of small repairs quoted as one day rate beats itemizing eleven tiny tasks.

blocks.h3: The license threshold — what you may legally quote as a handyman
paras: Most states cap unlicensed handyman work by dollar value, and quoting above the cap is itself a violation. California's $500 limit (labor and materials combined) is the best known; it means an unlicensed operator cannot legally accept a $600 fence repair even if the customer begs. Other states set the bar differently — Nevada distinguishes handyman work under $1,000 from contracting, Texas leaves general handyman work unregulated at the state level but cities often step in, and Florida requires a license for most structural work regardless of price.

The estimate is where this surfaces. If you are licensed, the license number goes on the quote — several states require it on any estimate or bid. If you are working under a threshold, keep each quote's total under the cap rather than splitting one job into multiple $499 estimates; regulators read split invoices as evasion, not compliance.

blocks.h3: Estimate vs. contract: when a quote becomes binding
paras: An estimate is a good-faith forecast; a fixed quote is an offer the customer can accept — and once accepted with a deposit, it functions as a contract for the work described. Handymen get into trouble by writing 'estimate' on a document and then treating it as a binding price, or the reverse. The clean pattern is to label the document explicitly and include three clauses that make either version safe: a valid-until date (materials prices move), a change-work clause (anything outside the listed scope is quoted separately), and a deposit line with a cap.

On deposits: many states regulate how much a contractor may collect up front. California caps deposits at $1,000 or 10% of the total, whichever is smaller, for licensed contractors — handymen quoting biggish jobs there collect material costs instead of a percentage. Write the deposit as a flat amount tied to materials, and the balance-due-on-completion line keeps the whole structure enforceable without a separate contract.

blocks.h3: The honey-do list: pricing a multi-task estimate without losing money
paras: The classic handyman job is a list: fix the garbage disposal, re-caulk two bathrooms, hang six pictures, patch the drywall dent, adjust two doors. Itemizing each task separately kills the quote — six lines of $40-$80 reads as nickel-and-diming, and small tasks priced individually always under-recover the setup and travel between them.

Working handymen quote the list as a package: one line per task for clarity, but the totals column shows a bundled labor figure, often as a day rate or half-day rate. The customer sees transparency (each task listed) while the math reflects reality (one trip, one setup, continuous work). The Excel version of this template supports both patterns — itemized lines that sum, or a single day-rate line with the task list in the description — and the 25% deposit row recalculates either way.

blocks.h3: Materials on the estimate: cost-plus with receipts
paras: Materials are where handyman estimates get contested, because the customer can check the hardware store price in thirty seconds. The convention that survives scrutiny is cost-plus-stated-percentage: list materials at cost on the estimate, add a disclosed markup line (10-20% is the customary range), and offer receipts on request. Some states' contractor rules expect markup to be identified as such rather than folded invisibly into a lump sum.

The alternative — a single 'materials allowance' line with a cap — works for quote-first jobs where you buy after approval: state the allowance, state that actual costs reconcile against it, and note whether overage requires written approval. Both patterns are easier to defend than a padded lump sum, and both keep the estimate's numbers matching the final invoice, which is the moment trust is actually tested.
